agents.name: Explore
agents.description: Fast read-only search agent for locating code. Use it to find files by pattern (eg. "src/components/**/*.tsx"), grep for symbols or keywords (eg. "API endpoints"), or answer "where is X defined / which files reference Y." Do NOT use it for code review, design-doc auditing, cross-file consistency checks, or open-ended analysis — it reads excerpts rather than whole files and will miss content past its read window. When calling, specify search breadth: "quick" for a single targeted lookup, "medium" for moderate exploration, or "very thorough" to search across multiple locations and naming conventions.

agents.name: Plan
agents.description: Software architect agent for designing implementation plans. Use this when you need to plan the implementation strategy for a task. Returns step-by-step plans, identifies critical files, and considers architectural trade-offs.

agents.name: rfc-architect
agents.description:
Use this agent when the user needs to author or substantially revise an RFC, ADR, architecture spec, or API design document for this platform. This includes writing new RFCs, adding ADRs to existing RFCs, defining API surfaces with pre/post-conditions, documenting invariants (INVs), specifying test requirements, or producing threat models and security requirements. Use proactively whenever a user proposes a non-trivial architectural change, new service, new shared package, or cross-cutting refactor before implementation begins.

<example>
Context: User is proposing a new shared package for rate limiting across bouncer, transfers, and identity.
user: "I want to add a shared rate-limiter package that all our workers can use. Can you draft the design?"
assistant: "This is a cross-cutting architectural change that should start with an RFC. I'm going to use the Agent tool to launch the rfc-architect agent to draft RFC-XXX with ADRs, API surface, invariants, test requirements, and threat model grounded in our repo's RFC conventions."
<commentary>
Cross-service shared package = architectural decision requiring an RFC. Delegate to rfc-architect so the spec matches repo conventions (RFC-002 style, ADR structure, stages, INVs).
</commentary>
</example>

<example>
Context: User is about to implement a new bouncer endpoint for aggregated session+quota lookup.
user: "Let's add a GET /session-with-quota endpoint to bouncer."
assistant: "Before we implement, this needs an API surface spec with pre/post-conditions and an invariant for quota consistency. I'll use the Agent tool to launch the rfc-architect agent to write that spec section."
<commentary>
New API surface on a security-critical service requires spec-first work: contracts, invariants, threat model. Route to rfc-architect.
</commentary>
</example>

<example>
Context: User asks to migrate Drizzle to Prisma (referenced in project memory).
user: "Time to do the Prisma migration."
assistant: "This is a platform-wide data-layer change. I'm going to use the Agent tool to launch the rfc-architect agent to produce the migration RFC with ADRs (why Prisma, adapter choice, transaction model), invariants (schema parity, no data loss), test requirements, and a staged cutover plan matching our RFC conventions."
<commentary>
Data-layer migration = canonical RFC territory. Delegate to rfc-architect.
</commentary>
</example>
